Hello LML, I would like to start making ongoing contributions in formalizing machine language algorithms. Couple of questions
1) Whats the relationship with CSlib? is there any overlap? would the work be upstreamed to CSlib at some point.
2) Going by the ideas listed in the presentation slides, would Linear bandits (algorithm, regret bound) be an acceptable algorithm to start formalizing?

For your question 2, yes linear bandits fit well with what we have done until now and would be a welcome contribution. You could look up the LinUCB algorithm in the Bandit Algorithms book, implement it and see what you need to prove a regret bound. Look at the UCB implementation for an example of bandit algorithm in our formalization.

Right now LML does not import CSLib but imports only Mathlib. Related to that, the repository contains only mathematical descriptions of algorithms, as sequences of Markov kernels that give the conditional laws of their output, but no link to actual implementations. This will change (hopefully soon) and we will import CSLib. I think that it is important that LML does not duplicate work done elsewhere and integrates well with the other packages, and we will use CSLib tools whenever we can. We should also make an effort to upstream any development that is not ML-specific (to CSLib or Mathlib), but it's fine to try things in our repository first.

started my first PR :) haven't gotten to regret bounds yet but feel free to comment, somewhat newbie to Lean. Also can you expand on "no actual implementations" from your comment. I imagine the implementations should be added, no?

I meant that our algorithms are not given as a block of code that you could run. We build a sequence of Markov kernels (or measurable functions from which we get a deterministic kernel) and call that an algorithm.
But ideally we should be able to write something that looks much more like the python code you would typically write to run the algorithm (and we would extract the kernel from there). See the discussion about do notation (at #Lean Machine Learning > Do notation for Giry monad but also other places on zulip) and discussions about typeclasses for Real and Float (#general > Typeclasses for Reals + Floats ).

I think I need a little bit of guidance here. proving linUCB end to end, seems an order of magnitude harder. Like I am using AI tools more than I would like frankly. I am trying to search for solutions in Mathlib but still it seems there is a lot of proof generation to be done for

  • feature vectors x_a : Fin d → ℝ,
  • design matrices V_t = λI + ∑ x_a x_aᵀ,
  • matrix inverses V_t⁻¹,
  • least-squares estimates θHat,
  • quadratic widths x_aᵀ V_t⁻¹ x_a,
  • determinant ratios det(V_t) / det(V_0),
  • elliptical potential bounds,
  • self-normalized concentration,
  • Gaussian-mixture/stopped-supermartingale scaffolding,
  • bridges from confidence ellipsoids to regret,
  • both high-probability and failure-probability theorem variants.
like is this expected? it seems like I have create many files/modules for sub proofs etc.
may be the PR would be a better place to discuss about it. https://github.com/LeanMachineLearning/LML/pull/113

I agree that it looks like a big piece of work! It seems doable from what we have (although possibly long), but it would not be surprising if many small helper lemmas need to be added to get to the end, or if you identify one big missing requirement.

It's probably a good idea to identify some parts of the work that can be developed in smaller, independent PRs. For example you could first try to prove the elliptical potential lemma in a separate PR. Or you could independently prove the regret bound (19.11) of the Bandit Algorithms book. That's the two main parts of proving the regret bound assuming Assumption 19.1, which is what is done in chapter 19. Then to prove that the assumption holds for LinUCB we will need to develop the method of mixtures as in chapter 20 of the book, which will be a large task on its own.

My advice is to choose one of those smaller parts and do that (or identify even smaller subparts), instead of trying to do the whole proof in one PR. And if you want you can open github issues for other parts of the proof for which you would like other people to help.

sounds good, I will subdividing this into several helper lemma files. I was looking for low hanging fruit and this is way way bigger but I think I have a lot of the pieces now so might as well take it to the finish line. I have absorbed the algorithms fairly well but there are several parts of the proofs which are AI assisted for which I understand the statements but not so much as the proofs. Hope that's ok

So the repo does not allow sub issues I think. It would be nice to have a parent linUCB issue and then sub issues linked to it. This is a very big module and can be subdivided into 8 sub issues at least
proved the regret bound for theorem 19.2 and the final high probability one as well with a lot of AI help. I am still going through to try understand the mechanics of it

Oh it does not allow sub-issues? I'll look for the option to allow them.
I see a create sub-issue button at the bottom of LML#112, so it might be a permission problem.
nope aint no button for me. feel free to create sub-issues if permissions is an issue.
I would prefer finding the setting to allow you to do it! But anyway, you don't need to have issues open before opening PRs, so feel free to open small PRs corresponding to those sub-issues.

Create a initial 3 stacked PRs now, you can review them, I will wait until they are reviewed and merged before issuing new ones, this will also give me time to understand what AI implemented downstream here :)
